body:
Why vaccination is needed

Infectious diseases are caused by organisms such as bacteria and viruses. The immune system protects the body through several mechanisms. Some defences are available from birth, while others develop after exposure to particular antigens.

Innate immunity provides broad, relatively rapid protection. Examples include the skin, certain protective secretions and immune cells that respond to invading organisms.

Acquired or adaptive immunity is more specific. B lymphocytes can produce antibodies, while T lymphocytes contribute to coordinated and cell-mediated immune responses. An important property of acquired immunity is the formation of immunological memory.

Vaccination: Administration of a vaccine to stimulate an immune response that can reduce the risk of a specified disease or its serious consequences.

How immune memory develops

A vaccine presents the immune system with an antigen, or with instructions that allow the body to produce an antigen. The immune system recognises this antigen as a target and develops an appropriate response.

During the initial response, selected immune cells multiply and participate in producing antibodies or other protective responses. Some become memory B cells or memory T cells. These memory cells can support a more rapid and effective response if the same antigen is encountered again.

Protection varies according to the vaccine, disease, age, health of the recipient and time since vaccination. A vaccine may reduce infection, severe disease or both. Vaccination does not necessarily provide complete or lifelong protection.

Active and passive immunity

FeatureActive immunityPassive immunity
Source of protectionThe person's own immune responseReady-made antibodies received from another source
How it developsAfter infection or vaccinationAfter maternal antibody transfer or antibody administration
OnsetUsually takes time to developCan provide relatively rapid protection
Immune memoryMay produce immune memoryTransferred antibodies do not themselves create immune memory

Maternal antibodies provide natural examples of passive immunity. Certain antibodies cross the placenta during pregnancy, and antibodies in colostrum help protect the newborn. Medically administered antibodies or antitoxins are other examples.

Antivenom used for snakebite contains antibodies directed against components of venom. It supplies ready-made antibodies rather than requiring the patient to develop new immune memory first. Similarly, certain antitoxin preparations can provide immediate antibody-based protection when clinically indicated.

Antigens, adjuvants and booster doses

An antigen is a substance recognised by the immune system. In vaccines it is commonly a component of a pathogen, a weakened or inactivated pathogen, or an antigen produced from vaccine-delivered genetic instructions.

Some vaccines contain an adjuvant, a substance that strengthens or shapes the immune response to the vaccine antigen. An adjuvant is not itself the disease-causing organism that the vaccine targets.

A booster dose is an additional dose given according to a recommended schedule to strengthen or maintain protection. Not every vaccine requires the same number of doses or boosters.

Vaccination and treatment have different purposes

Preventive vaccines are generally given before exposure to a disease or before the disease develops. Therapeutic medicines are given to treat an existing condition. Some vaccines may also be administered after exposure to reduce the risk of disease, depending on the infection and recommended schedule.

The important distinction is the purpose and mechanism of the product, not merely whether it is given by injection.

Prelims focus

  • Innate immunity is broad and present from birth; acquired immunity is antigen-specific.
  • B lymphocytes are associated with antibody production.
  • Vaccines generally stimulate active immunity and may generate immune memory.
  • Colostrum contains protective maternal antibodies, including IgA.
  • Antivenom supplies ready-made antibodies and is an example of passive antibody-based treatment.
  • Trap: Passive immunity can act rapidly, but it does not automatically generate the recipient's own immune memory.

[NCERT, Biology, Class XII, Chapter 8, Human Health and Disease, sections 8.2.1–8.2.4; World Health Organization, Vaccines and immunization: What is vaccination?, 22 October 2025, sections on vaccine function and protection, consulted 13 November 2026.]

title: Vaccines and Immunity: How the Body Develops Protection

body:
What is a vaccine platform?

A vaccine platform is the basic technological approach used to present an antigen to the immune system. Different platforms can aim to protect against the same disease, but they differ in what is administered and how the antigen becomes available to immune cells.

Some vaccines contain an entire weakened or inactivated organism. Others contain only a selected component. Newer approaches may deliver genetic instructions that allow the recipient's cells to produce a selected antigen.

Major vaccine platforms

PlatformWhat is administered?Example
Live attenuatedA living organism weakened so that it can stimulate immunity without ordinarily causing the disease in eligible recipientsBCG vaccine for tuberculosis
InactivatedAn organism rendered unable to replicateInactivated polio vaccine; Covaxin
Protein subunitSelected antigenic proteins or protein componentsRecombinant hepatitis B vaccine; Corbevax
ToxoidA bacterial toxin rendered non-toxic while retaining its ability to stimulate immunityTetanus toxoid-containing vaccines
Viral vectorA modified carrier virus containing genetic instructions for a selected antigenCovishield
mRNAMessenger RNA containing instructions to produce a selected antigenSelected COVID-19 vaccines, including Pfizer-BioNTech and Moderna products
DNADNA containing instructions to produce a selected antigenZyCoV-D

Whole-organism and protein-based vaccines

Live attenuated vaccines

A live attenuated vaccine contains a weakened organism capable of limited replication in the recipient. Such vaccines can stimulate a broad immune response. However, because they contain a living organism, some live vaccines may be unsuitable for people with particular forms of immunosuppression.

BCG is a live attenuated bacterial vaccine. Its inclusion in this category is a useful distinction: the word live does not mean that a vaccine must contain a virus.

Inactivated vaccines

An inactivated vaccine contains an organism that cannot replicate. It presents antigens to the immune system without relying on multiplication of the pathogen in the recipient. Depending on the vaccine, repeated doses or an adjuvant may be needed to achieve or maintain protection.

Covaxin, developed by Bharat Biotech, is an example of a whole-virion inactivated COVID-19 vaccine.

Protein subunit and toxoid vaccines

Protein subunit vaccines contain selected components rather than a complete organism. The recombinant hepatitis B vaccine contains hepatitis B surface antigen produced using recombinant technology, including production in yeast.

Corbevax is an Indian recombinant protein subunit COVID-19 vaccine. A toxoid vaccine differs from both a live and an inactivated whole-organism vaccine because it is based on a bacterial toxin whose harmful activity has been inactivated.

Vaccines that deliver genetic instructions

mRNA vaccines provide messenger RNA encoding a selected antigen. Cells use the delivered mRNA to make the antigenic protein, which can then stimulate an immune response. The vaccine does not need to contain a complete infectious pathogen.

DNA vaccines provide DNA instructions for production of an antigen. The information is expressed through cellular processes that include production of messenger RNA and then protein.

Viral vector vaccines use a carrier virus to deliver instructions for producing an antigen. The carrier is modified for vaccine use. A viral vector vaccine is therefore not the same as a vaccine containing the unmodified disease-causing virus.

An mRNA vaccine does not need to enter the cell nucleus to be translated into protein. Under ordinary vaccine action, it does not rewrite the recipient's DNA. DNA and viral-vector vaccines are different platforms and should not be assumed to behave identically.

Indian examples and the Gujarat connection

Covishield, manufactured in India by the Serum Institute of India, is based on a recombinant viral-vector platform. Covaxin uses an inactivated whole-virus platform. Corbevax uses a recombinant protein subunit platform. These products demonstrate that Indian vaccine manufacturing has employed several distinct technological approaches.

ZyCoV-D was developed by Zydus Cadila, associated with Ahmedabad, Gujarat, with support from the Department of Biotechnology and BIRAC. It received Indian emergency-use authorisation on 20 August 2021. The government described it at that time as the world's first DNA-based COVID-19 vaccine authorised for human use.

These are historical platform and authorisation facts. An emergency authorisation granted in 2021 does not, by itself, establish a product's routine availability, recommended use or authorisation status in November 2026.

What cannot be concluded from the platform alone?

No single vaccine platform is automatically the safest, most effective or most durable for every disease. Protection depends on the antigen, formulation, dose schedule, population studied and clinical evidence.

Similarly, neither the word recombinant nor the word genetic means that a vaccine necessarily contains a living pathogen. The material actually administered must be identified.

Prelims focus

  • BCG is a live attenuated bacterial vaccine.
  • Inactivated polio vaccine and Covaxin use inactivated organisms.
  • Recombinant hepatitis B vaccine and Corbevax are protein subunit vaccines.
  • Covishield is a viral-vector vaccine.
  • mRNA and DNA vaccines provide genetic instructions for making an antigen.
  • ZyCoV-D, developed by Ahmedabad-associated Zydus Cadila, received emergency-use authorisation on 20 August 2021.
  • Trap: A toxoid vaccine contains an inactivated toxin, not an inactivated whole bacterium.

[NCERT, Biology, Class XII, Chapter 8, Human Health and Disease, section 8.2.4; World Health Organization, The different types of COVID-19 vaccines, sections on live attenuated, inactivated, subunit, viral-vector and nucleic-acid platforms, consulted 13 November 2026; Press Information Bureau, Department of Biotechnology, DBT-BIRAC supported ZyCoV-D receives Emergency Use Authorization, 20 August 2021; Press Information Bureau, Department of Biotechnology, Year End Review 2021, sections on Corbevax and ZyCoV-D, December 2021.]

title: Vaccine Platforms: Live, Inactivated, Protein, Viral Vector, mRNA and DNA

body:
Why a successful vaccine must also be manufacturable

Discovering an antigen that can stimulate an immune response is only one part of vaccine development. A vaccine must also be manufactured consistently, evaluated for safety and effectiveness, stored appropriately and delivered to the people who need it.

Large-scale production requires a reliable supply of ingredients, suitable manufacturing facilities, trained workers, quality-testing systems and secure distribution arrangements. The exact production process differs between vaccine platforms.

From development to authorised use

Vaccine development ordinarily includes several stages:

  1. Preclinical evaluation: Laboratory and other non-human studies examine the proposed vaccine before clinical testing.
  2. Phase 1 clinical trials: Initial human studies examine safety, tolerability and immune responses in a relatively small group.
  3. Phase 2 clinical trials: Studies involving more participants further examine safety, immune responses and suitable vaccination schedules.
  4. Phase 3 clinical trials: Larger studies evaluate protection against the intended outcomes and gather further safety evidence.
  5. Regulatory review: The relevant authority assesses evidence about quality, safety and effectiveness before authorising specified uses.
  6. Post-authorisation monitoring: Manufacturers and health authorities continue evaluating safety, effectiveness and product quality.

During a public-health emergency, some development and review activities may proceed in parallel. This does not remove the need to examine supporting evidence. A product's regulatory authorisation is also distinct from its inclusion in a government's routine immunisation schedule.

Manufacturing and quality checks

Biological production may involve growing suitable cells or microorganisms, obtaining the vaccine material, purifying or inactivating it as required, combining it with other necessary components and packaging the final vaccine into vials or other suitable containers.

Quality control examines whether the vaccine meets relevant specifications, including identity, potency, purity, sterility where required and stability. Batch consistency matters because different production batches should meet the same approved quality requirements.

The steps after producing the main biological substance include purification, formulation and packaging. These activities are commonly associated with downstream processing.

Cold chain and vaccine distribution

Many vaccines lose effectiveness if exposed to temperatures outside their specified storage range. Maintaining suitable temperatures from manufacture to administration is called the cold chain.

Many vaccines require storage at 2–8°C, but this is not a universal requirement. Some vaccines need frozen or ultra-cold storage, while individual products have different permitted conditions after thawing or preparation. Storage must follow the requirements of the particular vaccine.

Regulation in India and international assessment

India's national medicines regulatory system includes the Central Drugs Standard Control Organisation (CDSCO), with the Drugs Controller General of India (DCGI) performing specified regulatory functions. Indian authorisation must not be confused with an assessment issued by the World Health Organization.

WHO prequalification assesses whether a vaccine meets applicable international requirements for procurement and programme use. WHO also has an Emergency Use Listing procedure for specified emergency circumstances. Neither procedure automatically replaces a country's own regulatory decisions.

Indian programmes that improve vaccine access

Universal Immunisation Programme

India's Universal Immunisation Programme (UIP) provides vaccines against specified vaccine-preventable diseases to eligible children and pregnant women through public health services. The programme aims to reduce disease and prevent avoidable deaths.

Mission Indradhanush

Mission Indradhanush, launched in 2014, focuses on improving immunisation coverage, particularly among children and pregnant women who have missed scheduled doses or remain insufficiently vaccinated.

eVIN and U-WIN

eVIN, the Electronic Vaccine Intelligence Network, supports vaccine supply management through information on stock and cold-chain temperatures. It concerns the availability and suitable storage of vaccines.

U-WIN is a digital platform for recording and following up vaccination of eligible beneficiaries under immunisation services. It supports registration, vaccination records and reminders. Nationwide rollout was announced in October 2024.

eVIN: Vaccine stocks and cold-chain management. U-WIN: Beneficiary vaccination records and follow-up. These systems serve different functions.

National Biopharma Mission

The National Biopharma Mission, launched in 2017, was a Department of Biotechnology initiative implemented through BIRAC to strengthen India's capacity for developing vaccines, biotherapeutics and related health technologies. The launch and stated objectives are historical facts; the original mission period should not be assumed to describe its operational status in 2026.

National HPV vaccination campaign and Gujarat

On 28 February 2026, India launched a nationwide campaign providing free, voluntary, single-dose human papillomavirus (HPV) vaccination for eligible girls aged 14 years at government health facilities. The campaign is intended to help prevent cervical cancer associated with HPV infection.

In a progress report dated 11 September 2026, the Ministry of Health and Family Welfare stated that India had administered more than 80 lakh doses under the campaign and that Gujarat had achieved 100% coverage of its identified target cohort. This was the reported status for that specified cohort and reporting date, not a claim that every girl in Gujarat had been vaccinated or that the percentage necessarily remained unchanged thereafter.

Why access remains a public-health issue

Scientific success does not guarantee equitable access. High prices, limited production capacity, procurement difficulties, shortages of trained personnel, poor transport, inadequate cold-chain equipment and lack of public awareness can prevent a vaccine from reaching eligible people.

Public procurement, domestic manufacturing, reliable supply management, outreach and affordable delivery help translate a biological innovation into population-level protection.

Prelims focus

  • Clinical development commonly includes Phase 1, Phase 2 and Phase 3 trials.
  • CDSCO and DCGI are associated with the Indian medicines regulatory system.
  • Many vaccines require 2–8°C storage, but temperature requirements are product-specific.
  • UIP delivers scheduled immunisation; Mission Indradhanush was launched in 2014 to improve coverage.
  • eVIN concerns vaccine stocks and temperatures; U-WIN concerns vaccination records.
  • The nationwide free HPV vaccination campaign for eligible girls aged 14 years began on 28 February 2026.
  • Trap: WHO prequalification, Indian regulatory authorisation and inclusion in UIP are separate decisions.

[NCERT, Biology, Class XII, Chapter 11, Biotechnology: Principles and Processes, section 11.3.6, Downstream Processing; World Health Organization, How are vaccines developed and produced?, 25 February 2025, sections on clinical trials, approval, packaging, storage and quality control; Press Information Bureau, Update on Universal Immunization Coverage, 13 February 2026; Press Information Bureau, Update on National HPV Vaccination Programme, 17 March 2026; Press Information Bureau, India Administers 80 Lakh HPV Vaccine Doses, 11 September 2026; Department of Biotechnology and BIRAC, National Biopharma Mission launch information, 2017; official programme information consulted 13 November 2026.]
